editorNote: The week opens with Compaq turning the IBM PC compatibility race into a portable-machine story while game shoppers see new console hardware, vector displays, and arcade conversions fighting for holiday attention.
morningLine: A 28-pound IBM-compatible portable, a built-in-vector console, and a horror anthology opening weekend make the computer counter feel crowded before Thanksgiving.

lead.headline: Compaq Turns PC Compatibility Into a Portable Pitch
lead.summary: Compaq announced its first Portable in November 1982, promising a luggable IBM PC-compatible machine built around a legally reverse-engineered BIOS. The $2,995-and-up system was not expected to ship until 1983, but the announcement signaled that IBM compatibility was becoming a market category, not just a single-company product line.
lead.confidence: Month-specific November 1982 product announcement; pricing and ship timing from historical Compaq Portable summaries.

computerItems.label: Console Counter
computerItems.headline: Vectrex Brings Its Own Vector Screen
computerItems.summary: General Consumer Electronics put the Vectrex into the crowded 1982 console field with a built-in monochrome vector monitor and plastic screen overlays, a sharp contrast to cartridge boxes fighting for the family television.

computerItems.label: Atari Desk
computerItems.headline: Atari 5200 Enters the Supersystem Race
computerItems.summary: Atari also pushed the 5200 SuperSystem in November, using Atari 8-bit computer-derived hardware and analog controllers as ColecoVision and Intellivision competed for holiday shelf space.

computerItems.label: Arcade Floor
computerItems.headline: Pole Position Keeps Racing Cabinets Busy
computerItems.summary: Namco and Atari's Pole Position remained one of 1982's defining arcade stories, using pseudo-3D racing and unusually powerful 16-bit arcade hardware for the period.
